chapters.title: The Gathering
paragraphs: I believe I am quite ready to answer what you ask. The day before yesterday I was walking up to the city from my home in Phalerum when an acquaintance of mine, who had spotted me from behind, called out playfully from some distance, 'Apollodorus, you Phalerian (Probably a play of words on (Greek), 'bald-headed.') — stop!' So I stopped, as he told me to. Then he said, 'Apollodorus, I was just looking for you. I wanted to ask about the speeches in praise of love that Socrates, Alcibiades and others gave at Agathon's supper. Phoenix, the son of Philip, heard about them from someone else and passed it on to me, but his account was very unclear. He said that you knew them, and I would like you to tell me what was said. Who has more right than you to report the words of your friend? But first, were you there at that gathering?'
'Glaucon,' I said, 'your informant must have been very unclear indeed, if you think the gathering took place recently, or that I could have been there.'
'Why, yes,' he replied, 'I did think so.'

'Impossible,' I said. 'Do you not know that Agathon has not lived in Athens for many years? And it has been less than three years since I got to know Socrates and began making it my daily business to know everything he says and does. Before that I ran about aimlessly, thinking I was doing something worthwhile, when in fact I was as wretched as anyone could be, no better than you are now. I thought I should do anything rather than be a philosopher.'
'Well,' he said, 'joking aside, tell me when the gathering took place.'
'When we were boys,' I replied, 'when Agathon won the prize with his first tragedy, the day after he and his chorus offered the sacrifice for the victory.'
'Then it must have been a long time ago,' he said. 'And who told you — was it Socrates?'

'No, indeed,' I replied, 'it was the same man who told Phoenix. He was a little fellow who never wore shoes, Aristodemus of the deme of Cydathenaeum. He had been at Agathon's feast, and I think that in those days no one admired Socrates more devotedly. I have also asked Socrates about parts of his account, and Socrates confirmed them.' 'Then,' said Glaucon, 'let us have the story again. Is the road to Athens not made for conversation?' So we walked and talked about the speeches on love. And that is why, as I said at the start, I am quite ready to do as you ask, and I will go over them again if you like. For I take the greatest pleasure in speaking about philosophy, or hearing others speak of it, quite apart from the benefit. But when I hear other talk, especially the talk of you rich men and traders, it annoys me, and I pity you, my companions, because you think you are accomplishing something when you are really accomplishing nothing. I suppose you pity me in return, and think me an unfortunate creature, and very likely you are right. But what you merely think about me, I know about you. That is the difference.

COMPANION: I see, Apollodorus, that you have not changed. You are always speaking ill of yourself and of everyone else. I do believe you pity all mankind except Socrates, and yourself first of all. You live up to your old nickname, though I do not know how you got it, Apollodorus the madman, whether or not you deserve it. You are always raging against yourself and everyone but Socrates.
APOLLODORUS: Yes, my friend, and the reason I am called mad and out of my wits is just that I hold these opinions about myself and about you. No other proof is needed.
COMPANION: Enough of that, Apollodorus. Let me ask again that you repeat the conversation.
APOLLODORUS: Well, the story of love went like this. But perhaps I had better begin at the beginning and try to give you the exact words of Aristodemus:
He said that he met Socrates fresh from the bath and wearing sandals. Since the sandals were unusual, Aristodemus asked him where he was going that he had made himself into such a beau.

'To a banquet at Agathon's,' he replied. 'I refused his invitation to the victory sacrifice yesterday, because I feared the crowd, but I promised to come today instead. So I have dressed up, because he is such a fine man. What do you say to coming along uninvited?'
'I will do as you tell me,' I replied.
'Follow, then,' he said, 'and let us wreck the proverb:
'To the feasts of inferior men the good unbidden go;'
and make it run instead:
'To the feasts of the good the good unbidden go;'

and Homer himself supports this change. He does not merely wreck the proverb, he outrages it. He pictures Agamemnon as the bravest of men, and Menelaus as a fainthearted warrior, yet he has Menelaus come unbidden (Iliad) to the banquet of Agamemnon, who is feasting and offering sacrifices. So the worse man goes to the better, not the better to the worse.'
'I am rather afraid, Socrates,' said Aristodemus, 'that this may still be my case, and that, like Menelaus in Homer, I shall be the inferior person who
'To the feasts of the wise unbidden goes.'
But I shall say that you invited me, and then you will have to make an excuse.'
'Two going together,'
he replied, in the manner of Homer, 'one or the other of them may invent an excuse on the way (Iliad).'

They talked in this way as they went along. Then Socrates fell behind, lost in thought, and told Aristodemus, who was waiting for him, to go ahead. When Aristodemus reached Agathon's house he found the doors wide open, and something comical happened. A servant came out, met him, and led him straight into the dining hall, where the guests were reclining, for the meal was about to begin. 'Welcome, Aristodemus,' said Agathon as soon as he appeared. 'You are just in time to eat with us. If you came about something else, put it off and join us. I was looking for you yesterday and meant to invite you, if I could have found you. But what have you done with Socrates?'
I turned around, but there was no sign of Socrates, and I had to explain that he had been with me a moment before, and that I had come at his invitation to the supper.
'You were quite right to come,' said Agathon, 'but where is he himself?'
'He was behind me just now, as I came in,' he said, 'and I cannot think what has become of him.'
'Go and look for him, boy,' said Agathon, 'and bring him in. And you, Aristodemus, take the place next to Eryximachus.'

The servant helped him wash, and he lay down. Presently another servant came in and reported that our friend Socrates had gone into the porch of the house next door. 'He is standing there,' said the servant, 'and when I call to him he will not move.'
'How strange,' said Agathon. 'Then you must call him again, and keep calling.'
'Leave him alone,' said my informant. 'He has a habit of stopping anywhere and losing himself for no reason. I believe he will soon appear, so do not disturb him.'

'Well, if you think so, I will leave him,' said Agathon. Then he turned to the servants and added, 'Let us have supper without waiting for him. Serve whatever you please, since no one is there to give you orders. I have never left you to yourselves before, but tonight imagine that you are our hosts, and that I and the company are your guests. Treat us well, and we shall praise you.' After this, supper was served, but still there was no Socrates. During the meal Agathon several times said he wanted to send for him, but Aristodemus objected. At last, when the feast was about half over, Socrates came in, for the fit, as usual, did not last long. Agathon, who was reclining alone at the end of the table, asked him to take the place next to him. 'So that I may touch you,' he said, 'and have the benefit of the wise thought that came to you in the porch and is now in your possession. I am sure you would not have come away until you had found what you were seeking.'

'How I wish,' said Socrates, taking the place he was offered, 'that wisdom could be passed by touch from the fuller person into the emptier, as water runs through wool from a fuller cup into an emptier one. If that were so, how greatly I would value the privilege of reclining at your side! You would fill me with a stream of wisdom, rich and beautiful. My own is of a poor and doubtful sort, no better than a dream. Yours is bright and full of promise, and it shone out in all the splendor of your youth the day before yesterday, in front of more than thirty thousand Hellenes.'

'You are mocking me, Socrates,' said Agathon. 'Before long you and I will have to settle which of us takes the prize for wisdom, and Dionysus will be the judge. But for now you had better attend to your supper.'

Socrates took his place on the couch and ate with the rest. Then libations were poured, a hymn was sung to the god, and the usual ceremonies were done. They were about to begin drinking when Pausanias said, And now, my friends, how can we drink with the least harm to ourselves? I can assure you that I am feeling the effects of yesterday's drinking badly, and I need time to recover. I suspect that most of you are in the same state, since you were at yesterday's party. So consider: how can we make the drinking easiest?
'I entirely agree,' said Aristophanes, 'that we should avoid hard drinking by all means. I was myself one of those who were drowned in drink yesterday.'
'I think you are right,' said Eryximachus, the son of Acumenus, 'but I would still like to hear one other person. Is Agathon able to drink hard?'
'I am not up to it,' said Agathon.

'Then,' said Eryximachus, 'it is lucky for weak heads like me, Aristodemus, Phaedrus and the others who can never drink, that the stronger ones are not in a mood for drinking. (I do not include Socrates, who can either drink or abstain and will not mind whichever we do.) Well, since none of the company seems disposed to drink much, I may be forgiven for saying, as a physician, that deep drinking is a bad practice. I avoid it when I can, and I certainly do not recommend it to anyone else, least of all to someone who still feels the effects of yesterday's carousing.'
'I always do what you advise,' rejoined Phaedrus the Myrrhinusian, 'and especially what you prescribe as a physician. And the rest of the company, if they are wise, will do the same.'
It was agreed that drinking would not be the order of the day, and that each person would drink only as much as he pleased.

'Then,' said Eryximachus, 'since you all agree that drinking is to be voluntary and that no one is to be forced, I move next that the flute-girl who has just come in be told to go away and play to herself or, if she likes, to the women inside (compare Prot.). Today let us have conversation instead. And if you will allow me, I will tell you what sort of conversation.' They accepted this proposal, and Eryximachus went on as follows.
'I will begin,' he said, 'in the manner of Melanippe in Euripides,
'Not mine the word'

that I am about to speak, but Phaedrus's. For he often says to me in an indignant tone: "What a strange thing it is, Eryximachus, that other gods have poems and hymns made in their honor, while the great and glorious god, Love, has no one to praise him among all the poets, though there are so many. There are the worthy sophists too, the excellent Prodicus for example, who have written in prose about the virtues of Heracles and other heroes. And, what is still more extraordinary, I have come across a philosophical work in which the usefulness of salt is the theme of an eloquent discourse, and many other such things have been honored in the same way. Think of it: people have taken such eager interest in these things, and yet to this day no one has dared to sing Love's praises as they deserve! This great deity has been entirely neglected." Now in this Phaedrus seems to me quite right. So I want to offer him a contribution, and I also think that, with all of us gathered here, we cannot do better right now than honor the god Love. If you agree with me, we will have no shortage of conversation. I propose that each of us in turn, going from left to right, give a speech in honor of Love. Let him give us the best he can. Phaedrus shall begin, because he is sitting first on the left and because he is the father of the idea.'

'No one will vote against you, Eryximachus,' said Socrates. 'How can I oppose your motion, when I claim to understand nothing but matters of love? I presume Agathon and Pausanias will not oppose it either, and there can be no doubt about Aristophanes, whose whole concern is with Dionysus and Aphrodite. Nor will anyone else I see around me disagree. The proposal, I am aware, may seem rather hard on those of us who sit last, but we shall be content if we first hear some good speeches. Let Phaedrus begin the praise of Love, and good luck to him.' All the company agreed, and asked him to do as Socrates told him.
Aristodemus did not remember everything that was said, and I do not remember everything he told me. But I will tell you what I thought most worth remembering, and what the chief speakers said.

chapters.title: Phaedrus's Speech
paragraphs: Phaedrus began by declaring that Love is a mighty god, wonderful among gods and men, and most wonderful in his birth. He is the eldest of the gods, and that is an honor to him. The proof is that no one records any parents of his, and no poet or prose writer has ever claimed that he had any. As Hesiod says:
'First Chaos came, and then broad-bosomed Earth, The everlasting seat of all that is, And Love.'
In other words, after Chaos these two came into being, the Earth and Love. Parmenides also sings of Generation:
'First in the train of gods, he fashioned Love.'

Acusilaus agrees with Hesiod. So there are many witnesses who acknowledge Love as the eldest of the gods. And he is not only the eldest, he is also the source of our greatest benefits. For I know of no greater blessing for a young man beginning life than a virtuous lover, or for a lover than a beloved youth. Men who mean to live nobly need a guiding principle, and neither family, nor honor, nor wealth, nor any other motive can plant it as well as love. What principle am I speaking of? The sense of honor and dishonor, without which neither states nor individuals ever accomplish anything good or great. Consider a lover who is caught doing something dishonorable, or who cowardly submits when another dishonors him. He will be more pained at being seen by his beloved than by his father, his companions or anyone else. The beloved, too, feels the same toward his lover when he is found in any disgraceful situation. Now if only there were some way to make a state or an army out of lovers and their beloved (compare Rep.), they would govern their own city better than anyone, avoiding all dishonor and competing with one another in honor. And fighting side by side, even a mere handful of them would overcome the whole world.

For what lover would not choose to be seen by all mankind rather than by his beloved when he is deserting his post or throwing away his weapons? He would rather die a thousand deaths than endure that. And who would abandon his beloved or fail him in the hour of danger? At such a moment even the biggest coward would become an inspired hero, the equal of the bravest, because Love would inspire him. Homer says that the god breathes courage into the souls of certain heroes. Love, by his own nature, puts that same courage into the lover.

Love will make men dare to die for their beloved, and love alone will do it, in women as well as men. Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, is proof of this to all Hellas. She was willing to give up her life for her husband when no one else would, though he had a father and a mother. Her love was so much more tender than theirs that she made them look like strangers to their own son, related to him in name only. The gods, like men, thought this act of hers so noble that, out of the many who have done virtuous deeds, they have granted only a very few the privilege of returning alive to earth, and she is one of them, in admiration of what she did. That is how greatly the gods honor the devotion and virtue of love. But Orpheus, the son of Oeagrus, the harper, they sent away empty-handed. They showed him only a phantom of the woman he sought and would not give her up, because he showed no spirit. He was only a harp-player, and he did not dare, like Alcestis, to die for love. Instead he schemed to enter Hades alive. And afterward they had him put to death by women, as the punishment for his cowardice.

Very different was the reward of Achilles for his true love toward his lover Patroclus. I say his lover and not his beloved (the notion that Patroclus was the beloved is a foolish error of Aeschylus, for Achilles was surely the more beautiful of the two, more beautiful than all the other heroes. And as Homer tells us, he was still beardless and far younger). The gods honor the virtue of love greatly, but they admire, value and reward even more the love that the beloved gives back to the lover. For the lover is more divine, since he is inspired by God. Now Achilles knew very well, because his mother had told him, that he could avoid death, go home and live to a good old age, if he did not kill Hector. Nevertheless he gave his life to avenge his friend, and dared to die, not only in his friend's defense but after his friend was dead. For this the gods honored him even above Alcestis and sent him to the Islands of the Blest. These are my reasons for saying that Love is the eldest, the noblest and the mightiest of the gods, and the chief author and giver of virtue in life and of happiness after death.

chapters.title: Pausanias's Speech
paragraphs: That, or something like it, was the speech of Phaedrus. Some other speeches followed which Aristodemus did not remember, and the next one he repeated was that of Pausanias. Phaedrus, he said, I do not think the subject has been set before us in quite the right form. We should not be called on to praise Love in such an undiscriminating way. If there were only one Love, what you said would be well enough. But since there is more than one Love, you should have begun by deciding which of them we were to praise. I will correct this fault. First I will tell you which Love deserves praise, and then I will try to praise that one in a manner worthy of him. We all know that Love is inseparable from Aphrodite, and if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love. But since there are two goddesses, there must be two Loves. And am I not right that there are two goddesses? The elder has no mother and is called the heavenly Aphrodite, the daughter of Uranus. The younger is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, and we call her the common Aphrodite. The Love who works with her is rightly called common, just as the other is called heavenly. All the gods ought to be praised, but not without distinguishing their natures, so I must try to distinguish the characters of the two Loves. Now actions differ according to the way they are performed.

Take what we are doing now, drinking, singing and talking. These actions are in themselves neither good nor evil. They turn out one way or the other according to how they are done. Done well, they are good, and done wrongly, they are evil. In the same way, not every love is noble and worthy of praise, but only the love that has a noble purpose. The Love who is the child of the common Aphrodite is common in his very nature and has no discrimination. He is the love felt by the lower sort of men, who are apt to love women as well as youths, and who love the body rather than the soul. The objects of this love are the most foolish people, for it desires only to reach its goal and never considers reaching it nobly, so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately. The goddess who is his mother is much younger than the other, and she was born from the union of male and female and shares in both. But the child of the heavenly Aphrodite comes from a mother in whose birth the female has no part. She comes from the male only. This is the love of youths, and since the goddess is older, there is no wantonness in her. Those inspired by this love turn to the male, and delight in the one who is braver and more intelligent by nature. Anyone can recognize the pure enthusiasts of this love by the very character of their attachments.

For they love not boys but intelligent beings whose reason is beginning to develop, at about the time their beards begin to grow. In choosing young men as companions they intend to be faithful to them and to spend their whole lives with them. They do not mean to take them in their inexperience, deceive them, make fools of them, or run off from one to another. But the love of young boys should be forbidden by law, because their future is uncertain. They may turn out good or bad, in body or in soul, and much noble enthusiasm may be wasted on them. In this matter the good are a law to themselves, but the coarser sort of lovers ought to be restrained by force, just as we restrain, or try to restrain, men from fixing their affections on women of free birth. These are the people who bring disgrace on love. Some have even been led to deny that such attachments are lawful because they see how improper and evil these are. But surely nothing that is done decently and lawfully can justly be criticized.

Now here and in Lacedaemon the rules about love are confusing, but in most cities they are simple and easy to understand. In Elis and Boeotia, and in countries with no gift for eloquence, they are very straightforward. The law simply favors these connections, and no one, young or old, has a word to say against them. The reason, I suppose, is that people in those parts are men of few words, so the lovers do not like the trouble of pleading their suit. In Ionia and other places, and generally in countries ruled by barbarians, the custom is considered dishonorable. Loves of youths share the bad name that philosophy and gymnastics have there, because they are hostile to tyranny. The interests of rulers require their subjects to be poor in spirit (compare Arist. Politics), and to have no strong bond of friendship or fellowship among them, which love, above all other motives, tends to inspire. Our Athenian tyrants learned this by experience, for the love of Aristogeiton and the constancy of Harmodius had a strength that destroyed their power.

So the bad reputation of these attachments should be blamed on the evil condition of those who gave them that reputation, that is, on the self-seeking of the rulers and the cowardice of the ruled. And on the other hand, the indiscriminate honor given to them in some countries is due to the laziness of those who hold that opinion. In our own country a far better principle prevails, but, as I was saying, it is rather hard to explain. Observe that open loves are held to be more honorable than secret ones, and that the love of the noblest and best is especially honorable, even if their persons are less beautiful than others. Consider also how much encouragement everyone gives the lover. He is not thought to be doing anything dishonorable. If he succeeds he is praised, and if he fails he is blamed. And in pursuing his love, custom allows him to do many strange things, which philosophy would sharply condemn if they were done from any motive of gain, or from a wish for office or power.

He may pray, plead and beg, swear oaths, lie on a mat at the door, and endure a slavery worse than any slave's. In any other case friends and enemies alike would be ready to stop him. But here there is no friend who will be ashamed of him and warn him, and no enemy who will accuse him of meanness or flattery. The actions of a lover have a grace that ennobles them, and custom has decided that they are highly commendable and that there is no loss of character in them. And strangest of all, he alone may swear and break his oath (so men say), and the gods will forgive his offense, for there is no such thing as a lover's oath. Such is the complete liberty that gods and men have allowed the lover, according to the custom of our part of the world. From this point of view a man may fairly argue that in Athens to love and to be loved is held to be very honorable. But consider how parents forbid their sons to talk with their lovers and put them under a tutor's care, who is appointed to see to these things. Their companions and equals taunt them with anything of the sort they observe, and their elders do not silence the critics or rebuke them. Anyone who reflects on all this will think, on the contrary, that we hold these practices to be most disgraceful.

But, as I was saying at the start, the truth, I imagine, is that it is not a simple question whether these practices are honorable or dishonorable. They are honorable to the man who follows them honorably, and dishonorable to the man who follows them dishonorably. It is dishonorable to yield to the evil man, or to yield in an evil manner, but honorable to yield to the good man, or to yield in an honorable manner. The vulgar lover is evil: he loves the body rather than the soul, and he is not even constant, because he loves a thing that is itself inconstant. So when the bloom of youth that he desired is over, he takes wing and flies away, in spite of all his words and promises. But the love of a noble character lasts a lifetime, for it becomes one with what is everlasting. Our custom wants both kinds of lovers to be tested well and truly. It would have us yield to the one sort and avoid the other, and so it encourages some to pursue and others to flee, testing both lover and beloved in contests and trials until they show which of the two classes each belongs to.

This is the reason why, first of all, a hasty attachment is held to be dishonorable: time is the true test of this, as of most other things. Second, there is dishonor in being overcome by the love of money, wealth or political power. A man may be frightened into surrender by the loss of them, or, having experienced the benefits of money and political corruption, he may be unable to rise above their temptations. For none of these things is permanent or lasting, to say nothing of the fact that no generous friendship ever sprang from them. So only one way of honorable attachment remains that custom allows in the beloved, and this is the way of virtue. We admitted that any service the lover does for the beloved is not to be counted as flattery or as a dishonor to himself. In the same way the beloved has only one way of voluntary service that is not dishonorable, and this is virtuous service.

For we have a custom that when anyone serves another because he thinks he will be improved by him in wisdom or in some other part of virtue, such voluntary service is not to be regarded as dishonorable and is not open to the charge of flattery. These two customs, the love of youth and the practice of philosophy and virtue in general, ought to meet in one. Then the beloved may honorably gratify the lover. For suppose the lover and the beloved come together, each with a law of his own. The lover thinks he is right to do any service he can for the one who gratifies him. The beloved thinks he is right to show any kindness he can to the one who is making him wise and good. The one is able to impart wisdom and virtue, and the other is seeking to acquire them for the sake of education and wisdom. When these two laws of love are fulfilled and meet in one, then and only then may the beloved honorably yield to the lover. And when love is disinterested in this way, there is no disgrace in being deceived. In every other case there is equal disgrace whether one is deceived or not. For suppose someone is gracious to his lover because he thinks him rich, and then is disappointed of his gains because the lover turns out to be poor. He is disgraced all the same, for he has done his best to show that he would give himself up to anyone's 'uses base' for the sake of money, and that is not honorable.

By the same principle, someone who gives himself to a lover because he is a good man, hoping to be improved by his company, shows himself to be virtuous, even if the object of his affection turns out to be a villain with no virtue. And if he is deceived, he has made a noble error. For he has shown that, for his part, he will do anything for anybody for the sake of virtue and improvement, and nothing can be nobler than that. So in every case it is noble to accept another for the sake of virtue. This is the love that belongs to the heavenly goddess. It is heavenly, and of great worth to individuals and cities, since it makes the lover and the beloved alike eager to improve themselves. All other loves belong to the other goddess, the common one. To you, Phaedrus, I offer this contribution in praise of love, as good as I could make it on the spur of the moment.

Pausanias came to a pause. This is the balanced way in which I have been taught by the wise to speak. Aristodemus said that Aristophanes was next, but either he had eaten too much or for some other reason he had the hiccough, and he had to change turns with Eryximachus the physician, who was reclining on the couch below him. 'Eryximachus,' he said, 'you must either stop my hiccough or speak in my turn until I have stopped.'

'I will do both,' said Eryximachus. 'I will speak in your turn, and you speak in mine. While I am speaking, let me recommend that you hold your breath. If after doing so for some time the hiccough is no better, gargle with a little water. If it still goes on, tickle your nose with something and sneeze. If you sneeze once or twice, even the most violent hiccough is sure to go.' 'I will do as you prescribe,' said Aristophanes, 'and now get on.'

chapters.title: Eryximachus's Speech
paragraphs: Eryximachus spoke as follows: Pausanias made a beautiful beginning but a lame ending, so I must try to make up what he left out. I think he was right to distinguish two kinds of love. But my own art teaches me something more. This double love is not only a feeling in the human soul toward the beautiful, or toward anything else. It is found in the bodies of all animals and in the produce of the earth, and I may say in everything that exists. This is the conclusion I seem to have drawn from medicine, which has shown me how great, how wonderful and how universal the god of love is, whose empire reaches over all things, divine and human alike. I will begin with medicine, to do honor to my art. The human body contains these two kinds of love. Everyone agrees that they are different and unlike, and being unlike, they have unlike loves and desires. The desire of the healthy is one thing and the desire of the diseased is another. Pausanias was just saying that it is honorable to indulge good men and dishonorable to indulge bad ones. In the same way, in the body, the good and healthy elements are to be indulged, while the bad elements, the elements of disease, are not to be indulged but discouraged.

This is what the physician must do, and in it the art of medicine consists. Medicine, taken generally, is the knowledge of the body's loves and desires, and of how to satisfy them or not. The best physician is the one who can tell beautiful love from foul love, or change one into the other. A skilled practitioner knows how to remove love and how to plant it, whichever is needed. He can also reconcile the most hostile elements in the constitution and make them loving friends. Now the most hostile elements are the most opposite ones: hot and cold, bitter and sweet, moist and dry, and the like. My ancestor Asclepius knew how to plant friendship and accord among these elements, and so he founded our art, as our friends the poets here tell us, and I believe them. Not only medicine in all its branches but also gymnastics and farming are under his rule. Anyone who gives the subject the slightest attention will see the same reconciliation of opposites in music. I suppose this must have been what Heracleitus meant, although his words are not exact. He says that The One is united by disunion, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre. But it is absurd to say that harmony is discord, or that it is made of elements that are still in discord.

What he probably meant was that harmony is made of differing notes, higher and lower, which once disagreed but have now been reconciled by the art of music. If the higher and lower notes still disagreed, there could be no harmony, clearly. For harmony is a symphony, and a symphony is an agreement. But an agreement of disagreements, while they still disagree, cannot exist. You cannot harmonize what disagrees. In the same way, rhythm is made of short and long elements that once differed and are now in accord. What medicine does in the first case, music does in all these others: it plants love and unison among them. So music too is concerned with the principles of love, as they apply to harmony and rhythm. Again, in the essential nature of harmony and rhythm there is no difficulty in seeing love, which has not yet become double. But when you want to use them in actual life, either in composing songs or in correctly performing airs or meters already composed (which is called education), then the difficulty begins, and the good artist is needed.

Then the old tale has to be told again, of beautiful and heavenly love, the love of Urania, the beautiful and heavenly muse. We must accept the temperate, and those who are not yet temperate only so that they may become so, and we must preserve their love. And we must tell of the vulgar Polyhymnia, who has to be used with care, so that the pleasure may be enjoyed without leading to licentiousness. It is the same in my own art, where it is a great matter to regulate the desires of the epicure so that he can gratify his tastes without the evil of disease that goes with them. From this I conclude that in music, in medicine, and in all other things, human as well as divine, both loves ought to be noted as far as possible, for both are present.

The course of the seasons is also full of both these principles. As I was saying, when the elements of hot and cold, moist and dry attain a harmonious love of one another and blend in temperance and harmony, they bring health and plenty to men, animals and plants, and do them no harm. But when the wanton love gets the upper hand and affects the seasons of the year, it is very destructive and injurious. It is the source of pestilence and brings many other kinds of disease on animals and plants. Hoar-frost, hail and blight come from the excesses and disorders of these elements of love, and to know them in relation to the revolutions of the heavenly bodies and the seasons of the year is called astronomy. Furthermore, all sacrifices and the whole province of divination, which is the art of communion between gods and men, are concerned only with preserving the good love and curing the evil love. For all kinds of impiety are likely to follow if a man, instead of accepting, honoring and revering the harmonious love in all his actions, honors the other love, whether in his feelings toward gods or parents, toward the living or the dead. So the business of divination is to look after these loves and heal them. Divination is the peacemaker between gods and men, working through a knowledge of the religious or irreligious tendencies that exist in human loves. Such is the great and mighty, or rather omnipotent, force of love in general.

And the love, more especially, that is concerned with the good, and is perfected in company with temperance and justice, whether among gods or men, has the greatest power. It is the source of all our happiness and harmony, and it makes us friends with the gods above us and with one another. I suppose I too have left out several things that might be said in praise of Love, but I did not do so on purpose. And you, Aristophanes, may now fill the gap or take some other line of praise, for I see that you are rid of your hiccough.

Yes, said Aristophanes, who spoke next, the hiccough is gone. It did not go, however, until I applied the sneezing. I wonder whether the harmony of the body loves such noises and ticklings, for as soon as I applied the sneezing I was cured.

Eryximachus said: Take care, my friend Aristophanes. You are about to speak, and yet you are making fun of me. I shall have to watch you, and see whether I cannot have a laugh at your expense, when you could have spoken in peace.

You are right, said Aristophanes, laughing. I take back my words. But please do not watch me. I am afraid that in the speech I am about to make, instead of others laughing with me, which is what our muse is born to and would be much better, I shall only be laughed at.
Do you expect to shoot your bolt and get away, Aristophanes? Well, perhaps if you are very careful, and remember that you will be called to account, I may be persuaded to let you off.

chapters.title: Aristophanes's Speech
paragraphs: Aristophanes announced that he would open another vein of discourse. He meant to praise Love in a different way from Pausanias or Eryximachus. Mankind, he said, judging by how they neglect him, have never, I think, understood the power of Love at all. If they had understood him, they would surely have built noble temples and altars for him and offered solemn sacrifices in his honor. But this is not done, and it most certainly ought to be, since of all the gods he is the best friend of men, the helper and healer of the ills that stand most in the way of the happiness of the race. I will try to describe his power to you, and you shall teach the rest of the world what I am teaching you. First, let me explain the nature of man and what has happened to it. Human nature originally was not what it is now, but different. There were not two sexes as there are now, but three at first. There was man, there was woman, and there was the union of the two, with a name matching this double nature. It once really existed but is now lost, and the word 'Androgynous' survives only as a term of reproach. Second, the primeval man was round, with his back and sides forming a circle. He had four hands and four feet, and one head with two faces, exactly alike, set on a round neck and looking in opposite directions. He also had four ears, two private parts, and everything else to match.

He could walk upright as men do now, backward or forward as he pleased. He could also roll over and over at great speed, turning on his four hands and four feet, eight in all, like tumblers going over and over with their legs in the air. This was how he ran fast. Now the sexes were three, and of the kind I have described, because the sun, moon and earth are three. The man was originally the child of the sun, the woman the child of the earth, and the man-woman the child of the moon, which is made up of sun and earth. They were all round, and they moved round and round like their parents. Their might and strength were terrible, and the thoughts of their hearts were great, and they attacked the gods. Of them is told the tale of Otys and Ephialtes, who, as Homer says, dared to scale heaven and would have laid hands upon the gods. Doubt reigned in the councils of the gods. Should they kill them and wipe out the race with thunderbolts, as they had done with the giants? Then there would be an end of the sacrifices and worship that men offered them. But on the other hand, the gods could not let such insolence go unchecked. At last, after a good deal of thought, Zeus found a way. He said: 'I believe I have a plan that will humble their pride and improve their manners. Men shall go on existing, but I will cut them in two. Then they will be weaker and more numerous, which will have the advantage of making them more profitable to us.

They shall walk upright on two legs, and if they stay insolent and will not keep quiet, I will split them again and they shall hop about on a single leg.' He spoke and cut men in two, like a sorb-apple halved for pickling, or like an egg divided with a hair. As he cut them one after another, he told Apollo to turn the face and half the neck around, so that each man would look at the cut side of himself and learn a lesson in humility. Apollo was also told to heal their wounds and put their shapes in order. So he turned the face around. He pulled the skin from the sides all over what in our language is called the belly, like a purse that draws shut, and made one mouth at the center, which he tied in a knot (the one we call the navel). He also smoothed the breast and took out most of the wrinkles, much as a shoemaker smooths leather on a last. He left a few, however, around the belly and navel, as a reminder of the primeval state. After the division, each of the two parts of man longed for its other half and came together with it. They threw their arms about one another and wrapped themselves in mutual embraces, longing to grow into one. They were on the point of dying from hunger and neglect of themselves, because they would not do anything apart. When one of the halves died and the other survived, the survivor looked for another mate and clung to that one, whether it was a man or a woman as we now call them, being the halves of whole men or whole women.

They were dying out, when Zeus in pity invented a new plan. He turned their organs of reproduction around to the front, for these had not always been there, and until then they had sowed their seed not in one another but in the ground, like grasshoppers. After this change, the male begot in the female, so that through the embraces of man and woman they might breed and the race might continue. And if man came to man, they might at least be satisfied, and rest, and go their ways to the business of life. So ancient is the desire of one another that is implanted in us, reuniting our original nature, making one of two, and healing the state of man. Each of us, when separated, having only one side, like a flatfish, is but the half of a man, cut in two like a tally, and he is always looking for his other half. Men who are a half of that double nature once called Androgynous are lovers of women. Adulterers are generally of this breed, and so are adulterous women who lust after men. Women who are a half of the original woman do not care for men but have attachments to women. The female companions belong to this class. But those who are a half of the male follow males. While they are young, being slices of the original man, they stay close to men and embrace them, and they are the best of boys and youths, because their nature is the most manly.

Some indeed say that they are shameless, but this is not true. They do not act this way from any lack of shame, but because they are brave and manly and have a manly look, and they embrace what is like them. And there is great proof of the truth of what I am saying: these are the only boys who, when they grow up, become statesmen. When they reach manhood they are lovers of youths, and they are not naturally inclined to marry or have children. If they do, it is only because the law requires it. They are content to live with one another unmarried. Such a nature is inclined to love and ready to return love, always embracing what is akin to it. And when one of them meets his other half, the real half of himself, whether he is a lover of youths or a lover of another sort, the pair are lost in a wonder of love, friendship and intimacy. Neither will be out of the other's sight, I may say, even for a moment. These are the people who spend their whole lives together, and yet they could not say what they want from one another. For the intense longing each has for the other does not seem to be the desire for lovers' intercourse, but for something else that the soul of each evidently desires and cannot name, and of which she has only a dark and uncertain presentiment.

Suppose Hephaestus, with his tools, came to the pair lying side by side and said to them, 'What do you people want of one another?' They would be unable to say. And suppose that, seeing their perplexity, he said: 'Do you desire to be wholly one, to be in one another's company always, day and night? If this is what you desire, I am ready to melt you into one and let you grow together, so that being two you become one. While you live you will live a common life as if you were a single man, and after your death in the world below you will still be one departed soul instead of two. I ask whether this is what you lovingly desire, and whether you will be satisfied to have it.' There is not one of them who, hearing the proposal, would deny it or would not admit that this meeting and melting into one another, this becoming one instead of two, was the very expression of his ancient need (compare Arist. Pol.). And the reason is that human nature was originally one and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love. There was a time, I say, when we were one. But now, because of the wickedness of mankind, God has scattered us, as the Arcadians were scattered into villages by the Lacedaemonians (compare Arist. Pol.).

And if we are not obedient to the gods, there is a danger that we shall be split up again and go about in basso-relievo, like the profile figures with only half a nose that are carved on monuments, and that we shall be like tallies. So let us urge all men to piety, that we may avoid evil and obtain the good, of which Love is to us the lord and minister. Let no one oppose him. Whoever opposes him is the enemy of the gods. For if we are friends of the God and at peace with him, we shall find our own true loves, which rarely happens in this world at present. I am serious, and so I must beg Eryximachus not to make fun of this or to see in it any allusion to Pausanias and Agathon, who, I suspect, are both of the manly nature and belong to the class I have been describing. But my words have a wider application. They include men and women everywhere. I believe that if our loves were perfectly fulfilled, and each of us, returning to his primeval nature, had his original true love, then our race would be happy. And if this would be best of all, then the next best thing, under present circumstances, must be the nearest approach to such a union, and that is to find a congenial love.

So, if we would praise the one who has given us this benefit, we must praise the god Love, who is our greatest benefactor. In this life he leads us back to our own nature, and he gives us high hopes for the future, for he promises that if we are pious he will restore us to our original state, heal us, and make us happy and blessed. This, Eryximachus, is my discourse on love. It is different from yours, but I beg you to leave it unassailed by the shafts of your ridicule, so that each may have his turn. Each, or rather either, for only Agathon and Socrates are left.

Indeed, I am not going to attack you, said Eryximachus, for I thought your speech charming. And if I did not know that Agathon and Socrates are masters in the art of love, I should be truly afraid that they would have nothing to say, after the world of things that have been said already. But for all that, I am not without hope.
Socrates said: You played your part well, Eryximachus. But if you were in my position now, or rather in the position I shall be in when Agathon has spoken, you would indeed be in a great strait.
You want to cast a spell over me, Socrates, said Agathon, in the hope that I will be thrown off balance by the expectation among the audience that I shall speak well.

I should be strangely forgetful, Agathon, replied Socrates, of the courage and generosity of spirit you showed when your own plays were about to be performed. You came onto the stage with the actors and faced the vast theater quite undismayed. It would be odd if I thought your nerves could be shaken by a small party of friends.
Do you think, Socrates, said Agathon, that my head is so full of the theater that I do not know how much more formidable a few good judges are to a man of sense than many fools?

No, replied Socrates, I should be very wrong to attribute to you, Agathon, that or any other lack of refinement. And I am quite sure that if you happened to meet anyone whom you thought wise, you would care for his opinion much more than for that of the many. But we, who made up part of the foolish many in the theater, cannot be counted as the select wise. Still, I know that if you were in the presence, not of one of us, but of some really wise man, you would be ashamed to disgrace yourself before him. Would you not?
Yes, said Agathon.
But before the many you would not be ashamed, if you thought you were doing something disgraceful in their presence?

Here Phaedrus interrupted them, saying: Do not answer him, my dear Agathon. If he can only get a partner to talk with, especially a good-looking one, he will no longer care about the completion of our plan. Now I love to hear him talk, but just at present I must not forget the encomium on Love that I am to receive from him and from everyone. When you and he have paid your tribute to the god, then you may talk.

Very good, Phaedrus, said Agathon. I see no reason why I should not go on with my speech, as I shall have many other chances to talk with Socrates. Let me first say how I ought to speak, and then speak:

chapters.title: Agathon's Speech
paragraphs: The previous speakers, instead of praising the god Love or unfolding his nature, seem to have congratulated mankind on the benefits he confers on them. I would rather praise the god first and then speak of his gifts. This is always the right way to praise anything. May I say, without impiety or offense, that of all the blessed gods he is the most blessed, because he is the most beautiful and the best? And he is the most beautiful, for, first, he is the youngest, and of his youth he is himself the witness. He flees from old age, which is swift enough, truly swifter than most of us like: Love hates old age and will not come near it. But youth and love live and move together, like to like, as the proverb says. Phaedrus said many things about Love with which I agree. But I cannot agree that he is older than Iapetus and Kronos. Not so: I maintain that he is the youngest of the gods, and ever young. The ancient doings among the gods of which Hesiod and Parmenides spoke, if the tradition of them is true, were done by Necessity and not by Love. Had Love been there in those days, there would have been no chaining or mutilation of the gods, no other violence, but peace and sweetness, as there is now in heaven, since the rule of Love began. Love is young, and he is also tender. He ought to have a poet like Homer to describe his tenderness, as Homer says of Ate that she is a goddess and tender:
'Her feet are tender, for she sets her steps, Not on the ground but on the heads of men:'

Here is an excellent proof of her tenderness: she walks not on what is hard but on what is soft. Let us offer a similar proof of the tenderness of Love. He walks not on the earth, nor yet on the skulls of men, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of both gods and men, which are the softest of all things. In them he walks, and dwells, and makes his home. Not in every soul without exception, for where there is hardness he departs, and where there is softness there he dwells. And since he nestles always, with his feet and in every way, in the softest of soft places, how can he be anything but the softest of all things? Truly he is the tenderest as well as the youngest, and he is also supple in form. If he were hard and could not bend, he could not enfold all things, or wind his way unnoticed into and out of every human soul. A proof of his suppleness and fine proportion is his grace, which everyone admits to be in a special way the attribute of Love, for ungracefulness and love are always at war with one another. The beauty of his complexion is shown by his dwelling among the flowers. For he does not dwell among beauties, of body or soul or anything else, that are bloomless or fading, but in the place of flowers and scents; there he sits and stays. Of the beauty of the god I have said enough, and yet much more remains that I might say.

Now I have to speak of his virtue. His greatest glory is that he can neither do wrong to any god or man nor suffer wrong from any. If he suffers, he does not suffer by force, for force does not come near him; and when he acts, he does not act by force. All men in all things serve him of their own free will, and where there is voluntary agreement, there, as the laws that are the lords of the city say, is justice. And he is not only just but exceedingly temperate. For Temperance is the acknowledged ruler of pleasures and desires, and no pleasure ever masters Love; he is their master and they are his servants. If he conquers them, he must be temperate indeed. As for courage, even the God of War is no match for him. The God of War is his captive and Love is the lord, for love, the love of Aphrodite, masters him, as the tale runs, and the master is stronger than the servant. And if he conquers the bravest of all others, he must himself be the bravest. Of his courage, justice and temperance I have spoken, but I have yet to speak of his wisdom, and I must try to do my best according to my ability. First, he is a poet (and here, like Eryximachus, I magnify my art), and he is also the source of poetry in others, which he could not be if he were not himself a poet.

At his touch everyone becomes a poet, even if he had no music in him before (A fragment of the Sthenoaoea of Euripides.). This too is a proof that Love is a good poet and accomplished in all the fine arts, for no one can give to another what he does not have himself, or teach what he does not know. Who will deny that the creation of the animals is his doing? Are they not all the works of his wisdom, born and begotten of him? And as for the artists, do we not know that only the one whom love inspires has the light of fame? The one whom Love does not touch walks in darkness. The arts of medicine, archery and divination were discovered by Apollo, guided by love and desire, so that he too is a disciple of Love. The melody of the Muses, the metalwork of Hephaestus, the weaving of Athene, and the rule of Zeus over gods and men are also all due to Love, who was their inventor. So Love set the empire of the gods in order, the love of beauty, as is evident, for with deformity Love has no concern. In the days of old, as I said at the start, dreadful deeds were done among the gods, for they were ruled by Necessity. But now, since the birth of Love, and from the Love of the beautiful, every good has sprung up in heaven and earth. Therefore, Phaedrus, I say that Love is the most beautiful and best in himself, and the cause of what is most beautiful and best in all other things. And a line of poetry comes into my mind in which he is called the god who
'Gives peace on earth and calms the stormy deep, Who stills the winds and bids the sufferer sleep.'

This is he who empties men of ill feeling and fills them with affection, who brings them together at banquets such as this. In sacrifices, feasts and dances he is our lord. He sends courtesy and sends away discourtesy; he always gives kindness and never gives unkindness; the friend of the good, the wonder of the wise, the amazement of the gods; desired by those who have no share in him, and precious to those who have the better share in him; parent of delicacy, luxury, desire, fondness, softness, grace; regardful of the good, regardless of the evil; in every word, work, wish and fear, savior, pilot, comrade, helper; glory of gods and men, leader best and brightest: in whose footsteps let every man follow, sweetly singing in his honor and joining in that sweet strain with which love charms the souls of gods and men. Such is the speech, Phaedrus, half playful, yet with a certain measure of seriousness, which, to the best of my ability, I dedicate to the god.

When Agathon had finished speaking, Aristodemus said that there was a general cheer. The young man was thought to have spoken in a way worthy of himself and of the god. And Socrates, looking at Eryximachus, said: Tell me, son of Acumenus, was there not reason in my fears? Was I not a true prophet when I said that Agathon would make a wonderful speech and that I should be in a strait?
The part of the prophecy that concerns Agathon, replied Eryximachus, seems to me to be true. But not the other part, that you will be in a strait.

Why, my dear friend, said Socrates, must not I, or anyone, be in a strait who has to speak after hearing such a rich and varied speech? I am especially struck by the beauty of the closing words. Who could listen to them without amazement? When I thought of how immeasurably inferior my own powers are, I was ready to run away for shame, if there had been any way to escape. For I was reminded of Gorgias, and at the end of his speech I fancied that Agathon was shaking at me the Gorginian or Gorgonian head of that great master of rhetoric, which was simply to turn me and my speech into stone, as Homer says (Odyssey), and strike me dumb. Then I saw how foolish I had been to agree to take my turn with you in praising love, and to say that I too was a master of the art, when I really had no conception of how anything ought to be praised. In my simplicity I imagined that the topics of praise should be true, and that, this being assumed, the speaker was to choose the best of the true things and set them forth in the best manner. I felt quite proud, thinking that I knew the nature of true praise and would speak well. But now I see that the plan was to attribute to Love every kind of greatness and glory, whether it really belonged to him or not, without regard to truth or falsehood. That did not matter. For the original proposal seems to have been, not that each of you should really praise Love, but only that you should appear to praise him.

And so you attribute to Love every imaginable form of praise that can be gathered anywhere. You say that 'he is all this,' and 'the cause of all that,' making him appear the most beautiful and best of all to those who do not know him, for you cannot fool those who do. And you have delivered a noble and solemn hymn of praise. But I misunderstood the nature of praise when I said that I would take my turn, and so I must beg to be released from the promise I made in ignorance, which (as Euripides would say (Eurip. Hyppolytus)) was a promise of the lips and not of the mind. Farewell, then, to such a strain, for I do not praise in that way. No, indeed, I cannot. But if you would like to hear the truth about love, I am ready to speak in my own manner, though I will not make myself ridiculous by entering into any rivalry with you. Tell me then, Phaedrus, whether you would like to have the truth about love, spoken in whatever words and in whatever order happen to come into my mind at the time. Will that be agreeable to you?

Aristodemus said that Phaedrus and the company told him to speak in whatever manner he thought best. Then, he added, let me have your permission first to ask Agathon a few more questions, so that I may take his admissions as the premises of my discourse.
I grant the permission, said Phaedrus: put your questions. Socrates then went on as follows:

chapters.title: Socrates & Diotima
paragraphs: You spoke magnificently just now, my dear Agathon, and I think you were right to propose speaking first about the nature of Love and afterward about his works. I very much approve of that way of beginning. Since you have described his nature so eloquently, let me ask you something more: is love the love of something, or of nothing? I must explain what I mean. I am not asking whether it is the love of a father or of a mother, which would be ridiculous. I mean it as I would ask: is a father a father of something? You would have no difficulty answering, of a son or a daughter, and that answer would be right.
True, said Agathon.
And you would say the same of a mother?
He agreed.
Let me ask one more question to make my meaning clear: is a brother not essentially a brother of something?
Certainly, he replied.
Of a brother or sister, that is?
Yes, he said.
And now, said Socrates, I will ask about Love: is Love the love of something, or of nothing?
Of something, surely, he replied.
Hold on to what that something is, and tell me what I want to know: does Love desire the thing that love is of?
Yes, surely.
And does he have the thing he loves and desires, or does he not have it?
Probably not, I would say.

No, replied Socrates, consider whether 'necessarily' is not the better word. In my judgment, Agathon, it is absolutely and necessarily true that whoever desires something lacks it, and that whoever desires nothing lacks nothing. What do you think?
I agree with you, said Agathon.
Good. Would a man who is great desire to be great, or a man who is strong desire to be strong?
That would contradict what we have already admitted.
True. For someone who is a certain thing cannot lack that very thing, can he?
That's right.

And yet, added Socrates, suppose a man who is strong desired to be strong, or a man who is swift desired to be swift, or a man who is healthy desired to be healthy. In that case someone might think he desires something he already has or is. I give these examples so that we avoid a misunderstanding. For the people who have these qualities, Agathon, must be taken to have their advantages at the moment, whether they choose to or not. And who can desire what he has? So when a person says, 'I am well and I wish to be well,' or 'I am rich and I wish to be rich,' or 'I simply desire to have what I have,' we shall reply: 'My friend, you have wealth and health and strength, and you want to keep them. For at this moment, whether you choose to or not, you have them. So when you say, "I desire what I have and nothing else," do you not mean that you want to have in the future what you have now?' He must agree with us, must he not?
He must, replied Agathon.
Then, said Socrates, he desires that what he has now be kept for him in the future. That is the same as saying that he desires something that does not yet exist for him, something he has not yet got.
That's very true, he said.

Then he, and everyone who desires, desires what he does not already have: something future and not present, something he does not have, and is not, and lacks. These are the sort of things that love and desire seek?
Very true, he said.
Then let us go back over the argument, said Socrates. First, is love not of something, and of something that a man lacks?
Yes, he replied.

Now remember what you said in your speech, or if you do not remember I will remind you. You said that the love of the beautiful set the empire of the gods in order, because there is no love of ugly things. Did you not say something like that?
Yes, said Agathon.
Yes, my friend, and the remark was just. And if that is true, Love is the love of beauty and not of ugliness?
He agreed.
And we have already admitted that Love is of something a man lacks and does not have?
True, he said.
Then Love lacks beauty and does not have it?
Certainly, he replied.
And would you call something beautiful if it lacks beauty and does not possess it?
Certainly not.
Then would you still say that love is beautiful?
Agathon replied: I fear I did not understand what I was saying.
It was a very good speech, Agathon, replied Socrates. But there is one more small question I would like to ask: is the good not also the beautiful?
Yes.
Then if love lacks the beautiful, it lacks the good as well?
I cannot refute you, Socrates, said Agathon. Let us take it that what you say is true.
Say rather, beloved Agathon, that you cannot refute the truth. Socrates is easy enough to refute.

And now I will take my leave of you and repeat a tale about love that I heard from Diotima of Mantineia (compare 1 Alcibiades). She was a woman wise in this and in many other kinds of knowledge. Once, in the days of old, when the Athenians offered sacrifice before the plague came, she delayed the disease for ten years. She was my teacher in the art of love, and I shall repeat what she told me. I will begin with the admissions Agathon made, which are nearly, if not exactly, the same as those I made to the wise woman when she questioned me. I think this will be the easiest way, and I shall play both parts myself as best I can (compare Gorgias). As you suggested, Agathon (supra), I must speak first of the being and nature of Love, and then of his works. I began by telling her, in nearly the same words he used to me, that Love was a mighty god and also beautiful. And she proved to me, as I proved to him, that by my own account Love was neither beautiful nor good. 'What do you mean, Diotima?' I said. 'Is love then evil and ugly?' 'Hush,' she cried. 'Must something be ugly just because it is not beautiful?' 'Certainly,' I said. 'And is whatever is not wise ignorant? Do you not see that there is something in between wisdom and ignorance?' 'And what may that be?' I said.

'Right opinion,' she replied. 'As you know, it cannot give a reason, so it is not knowledge (for how can knowledge be without reason?). Nor is it ignorance (for ignorance cannot reach the truth). It is clearly something in between ignorance and wisdom.' 'Quite true,' I replied. 'Then do not insist,' she said, 'that whatever is not beautiful is necessarily ugly, or that whatever is not good is evil. And do not conclude that because love is not beautiful and good he must be ugly and evil. He is in between them.' 'Well,' I said, 'surely everyone admits that Love is a great god.' 'Everyone who knows, or everyone who does not know?' 'Everyone.' 'And how, Socrates,' she said with a smile, 'can Love be acknowledged a great god by those who say he is not a god at all?' 'And who are they?' I said. 'You and I are two of them,' she replied. 'How can that be?' I said. 'It is quite easy to understand,' she replied. 'You yourself would admit that the gods are happy and beautiful. Of course you would. Would you dare to say that any god was not?' 'Certainly not,' I replied. 'And by the happy you mean those who possess good and beautiful things?' 'Yes.' 'And you admitted that Love, because he lacks them, desires the good and beautiful things that he lacks?' 'Yes, I did.' 'But how can he be a god if he has no share in what is good or beautiful?' 'He cannot.' 'Then you see that you too deny that Love is divine.'

'What then is Love?' I asked. 'Is he mortal?' 'No.' 'What then?' 'As before, he is neither mortal nor immortal, but in between the two.' 'What is he, Diotima?' 'He is a great spirit (daimon), and like all spirits he stands between the divine and the mortal.' 'And what,' I said, 'is his power?' 'He interprets,' she replied, 'between gods and men. He carries to the gods the prayers and sacrifices of men, and he brings to men the commands and replies of the gods. He is the mediator who bridges the gap between them, and so in him everything is bound together. Through him come the arts of the prophet and the priest, their sacrifices and mysteries and charms, and all prophecy and incantation. For God does not mingle with man. It is through Love that all the dealings and conversation between God and man, waking or sleeping, are carried on. The wisdom that understands this is spiritual; all other wisdom, such as that of the arts and crafts, is low and vulgar. Now these spirits, or intermediate powers, are many and various, and one of them is Love.' 'And who,' I said, 'was his father, and who his mother?' 'It will take some time to tell,' she said, 'but I will tell you. On the birthday of Aphrodite the gods held a feast. Among the guests was the god Poros or Plenty, who is the son of Metis or Discretion. When the feast was over, Penia or Poverty, as usually happens on such occasions, came to the doors to beg.

Now Plenty, who had had too much nectar (there was no wine in those days), went into the garden of Zeus and fell into a heavy sleep. Poverty, thinking of her own hard circumstances, plotted to have a child by him. So she lay down at his side and conceived Love. Love is the follower and attendant of Aphrodite, partly because he is by nature a lover of the beautiful and Aphrodite herself is beautiful, and partly because he was born on her birthday. And his fortunes match his parentage. First of all, he is always poor, and far from the tender and beautiful creature most people imagine. He is rough and filthy, with no shoes and no house to live in. He lies on the bare ground, exposed under the open sky, in the streets or at people's doors, taking his rest. Like his mother, he is always in need. Like his father, whom he also partly resembles, he is always plotting against the beautiful and good. He is bold, enterprising and strong, a mighty hunter, always weaving some scheme, keen in the pursuit of wisdom, rich in resources, a philosopher at all times, terrible as an enchanter, sorcerer and sophist. By nature he is neither mortal nor immortal. In one moment, when he has plenty, he is alive and flourishing; in the next he is dead; and then he is alive again, thanks to his father's nature.

But what flows in always flows out, so he is never without means and never wealthy. He is also in between ignorance and knowledge. The truth of the matter is this. No god is a philosopher or seeker after wisdom, for he is wise already. Nor does any man who is wise seek wisdom. Neither do the ignorant seek wisdom. For this is the evil of ignorance: someone who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself. He has no desire for what he does not feel he lacks.' 'But who then, Diotima,' I said, 'are the lovers of wisdom, if they are neither the wise nor the foolish?' 'A child could answer that,' she replied. 'They are those in between the two, and Love is one of them. For wisdom is a most beautiful thing, and Love is of the beautiful. Therefore Love is also a philosopher, a lover of wisdom, and being a lover of wisdom he is in between the wise and the ignorant. His birth is the cause of this as well: his father is wealthy and wise, and his mother poor and foolish. Such, my dear Socrates, is the nature of the spirit Love. Your mistake about him was very natural. As I gather from what you say, it came from confusing love with the beloved, which made you think love was all beautiful. For the beloved is the truly beautiful, and delicate, and perfect, and blessed. But the principle of love is of another nature, and is as I have described.'

I said, 'You, stranger woman, speak well. But if Love is as you say, what use is he to men?' 'That, Socrates,' she replied, 'I will try to explain. I have already told you of his nature and birth, and you agree that love is of the beautiful. But someone will ask: of the beautiful in what, Socrates and Diotima? Or rather, let me put the question more clearly: when a man loves the beautiful, what does he desire?' I answered her, 'That the beautiful may be his.' 'Still,' she said, 'your answer raises another question: what does a man get by having beauty?' 'I have no answer ready for what you ask,' I replied. 'Then,' she said, 'let me put the word "good" in place of the beautiful and ask again: if he who loves loves the good, what is it that he loves?' 'The possession of the good,' I said. 'And what does he gain who possesses the good?' 'Happiness,' I replied. 'That is easier to answer.' 'Yes,' she said, 'the happy are made happy by acquiring good things. And there is no need to ask why a man desires happiness. The answer is already final.' 'You are right,' I said.

'And is this wish and this desire common to all? Do all men always desire their own good, or only some men? What do you say?' 'All men,' I replied. 'The desire is common to all.' 'Why, then,' she went on, 'Socrates, are not all men said to love, but only some? You say that all men are always loving the same things.' 'I wonder about that myself,' I said. 'There is nothing to wonder at,' she replied. 'One part of love has been set apart and given the name of the whole, while the other parts have other names.' 'Give an example,' I said. She answered me as follows: 'Take poetry, which, as you know, is complex and many-sided. All creation, every passage of non-being into being, is poetry or making. The processes of all the arts are creative, and the masters of the arts are all poets or makers.' 'Very true.' 'Yet,' she said, 'you know they are not called poets. They have other names. Only the one portion of the art that has been set apart from the rest, the part concerned with music and meter, is called poetry, and those who practice poetry in this sense are called poets.' 'Very true,' I said. 'And it is the same with love.

In general you may say that all desire for good and happiness is simply the great and subtle power of love. But those who are drawn toward him by some other path, whether the path of money-making or gymnastics or philosophy, are not called lovers. The name of the whole is given to those whose affection takes one form only. They alone are said to love, or to be lovers.' 'I dare say you are right,' I replied. 'Yes,' she added, 'and you hear people say that lovers are looking for their other half. But I say that they are looking neither for the half of themselves nor for the whole, unless the half or the whole is also good. People will cut off their own hands and feet and throw them away if they are bad. For they do not love what is their own, unless perhaps someone calls what belongs to him the good and what belongs to another the evil. For there is nothing men love but the good. Is there anything?' 'Certainly, I would say there is nothing.' 'Then,' she said, 'the simple truth is that men love the good.' 'Yes,' I said. 'And we must add that they love to possess the good?' 'Yes, that must be added.' 'And not only to possess it, but to possess it forever?' 'That must be added too.' 'Then love,' she said, 'can be described in general as the love of possessing the good forever?' 'That is most true.'

'Then if this is the nature of love, can you tell me further,' she said, 'how it goes about its pursuit? What are people doing when they show all this eagerness and heat that we call love? And what is the aim they have in view? Answer me.' 'No, Diotima,' I replied. 'If I had known, I would not be amazed at your wisdom, and I would not have come to you to learn about this very matter.' 'Well,' she said, 'I will teach you. The aim they have in view is birth in beauty, whether of body or of soul.' 'I do not understand you,' I said. 'The oracle needs explaining.' 'I will make my meaning clearer,' she replied. 'I mean that all men are bringing to birth, in their bodies and in their souls. There comes a certain age at which human nature desires to procreate. This procreation must be in beauty and not in ugliness. It is the union of man and woman, and it is a divine thing. For conception and generation are an immortal principle in the mortal creature, and they can never take place where there is no harmony. But the ugly is always out of harmony with the divine, and the beautiful is in harmony with it.

Beauty, then, is the destiny or goddess of childbirth who presides at the birth. So when the power of conception approaches beauty, it becomes gracious and expansive and kindly, and it begets and bears fruit. At the sight of ugliness it frowns and contracts and feels pain, and it turns away and shrivels up, and not without a pang holds back from conceiving. This is why, when the hour of conception arrives and the teeming nature is full, there is such a flutter and ecstasy around beauty, whose approach relieves the pain of labor. For love, Socrates, is not, as you imagine, the love of the beautiful only.' 'What then?' 'The love of generation and of birth in beauty.' 'Yes,' I said. 'Yes, indeed,' she replied. 'But why of generation?' 'Because to a mortal creature generation is a kind of eternity and immortality,' she replied. 'And if, as we have already admitted, love is of possessing the good forever, then all men will necessarily desire immortality together with the good. Therefore love is of immortality.'

All this she taught me at various times when she spoke of love. I remember her once saying to me, 'What is the cause of love, Socrates, and of the desire that goes with it? Do you not see how all animals, birds as well as beasts, are in agony when they catch the infection of love in their desire to procreate? It begins with the desire for union, and then comes care for the young. For their sake the weakest are ready to fight against the strongest, even to the utmost, and to die for them. They will let themselves be tormented with hunger, or suffer anything, to keep their young alive. One might suppose that men act like this from reason. But why should animals have such passionate feelings? Can you tell me why?' Again I replied that I did not know. She said to me, 'And do you expect ever to become a master in the art of love if you do not know this?' 'But I have told you already, Diotima, that I come to you because of my ignorance. I know that I need a teacher. Tell me then the cause of this and of the other mysteries of love.' 'Do not be amazed,' she said, 'if you believe that love is of the immortal, as we have several times agreed. For here again, on the same principle, the mortal nature is seeking, as far as it can, to be everlasting and immortal. It can only reach this through generation, because generation always leaves behind a new existence in place of the old.

Even within the life of a single individual there is succession and not absolute unity. A man is called the same, yet in the short interval between youth and old age, during which every animal is said to have life and identity, he is going through a constant process of loss and repair. Hair, flesh, bones, blood, the whole body, are always changing. This is true not only of the body but also of the soul. Its habits, tempers, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains and fears never stay the same in any one of us but are always coming and going. It is equally true of knowledge, and what is still more surprising to us mortals, the sciences in general not only spring up and decay, so that in regard to them we are never the same, but each one of them individually goes through the same change. For what is meant by the word "recollection" but the departure of knowledge, which is always being forgotten, and is renewed and preserved by recollection? It appears to be the same although in reality it is new. This follows the law of succession by which all mortal things are preserved: not by remaining absolutely the same, but by substitution, the old worn-out mortality leaving behind another new and similar existence. The divine is unlike this, for it is always the same and never another. And in this way, Socrates, the mortal body, or any mortal thing, shares in immortality, while the immortal shares in it in another way.
Do not be amazed, then, at the love all men have for their offspring. That universal love and concern is for the sake of immortality.'

I was astonished at her words and said, 'Is this really true, O wise Diotima?' And with all the authority of an accomplished sophist she answered: 'Of that, Socrates, you may be sure. Just think of the ambition of men, and you will wonder at the senselessness of their ways, unless you consider how they are stirred by the love of immortal fame.
