They are ready to run all risks, far greater than they would run for their children, to spend money, to undergo any kind of toil, and even to die, for the sake of leaving behind a name that will be eternal. Do you imagine that Alcestis would have died to save Admetus, or Achilles to avenge Patroclus, or your own Codrus to preserve the kingdom for his sons, if they had not imagined that the memory of their virtues, which still survives among us, would be immortal? No,' she said, 'I am convinced that all men do all things, and the better they are the more they do them, in hope of the glorious fame of immortal virtue. For they desire the immortal.

'Those who are pregnant in the body only turn to women and beget children. This is the character of their love. They hope that their offspring will preserve their memory and give them the blessedness and immortality that they desire for the future. But there are those who are pregnant in soul, for certainly there are men who are more creative in their souls than in their bodies. They conceive what is proper for the soul to conceive or contain. And what are these conceptions? Wisdom and virtue in general. Such creators are the poets and all artists who deserve the name of inventor. But by far the greatest and most beautiful kind of wisdom is the kind concerned with the ordering of states and families, which is called temperance and justice. And when someone has had the seed of these implanted in him from youth, and is himself inspired, he desires on reaching maturity to beget and bring forth.

He wanders about looking for beauty in which he may beget offspring, for in ugliness he will beget nothing. Naturally he embraces beautiful bodies rather than ugly ones. Above all, when he finds a beautiful and noble and well-nurtured soul, he embraces both in one person. To such a person he is full of talk about virtue, and about the nature and pursuits of a good man, and he tries to educate him. At the touch of the beautiful, which is always present to his memory even when the other is absent, he brings forth what he had conceived long before. Together they raise what he has brought forth. They are married by a far closer tie and a firmer friendship than those who beget mortal children, because the children they share are more beautiful and more immortal. Who, thinking of Homer and Hesiod and the other great poets, would not rather have their children than ordinary human ones? Who would not wish to rival them in producing children like theirs, which have preserved their memory and given them everlasting glory? Or who would not want children like those Lycurgus left behind him, the saviors, one may say, not only of Lacedaemon but of Hellas?

There is Solon too, the revered father of the Athenian laws. And there are many others in many other places, among Hellenes and barbarians alike, who have given the world many noble works and been the parents of every kind of virtue. Many temples have been raised in their honor because of children like theirs, whereas none were ever raised to anyone for the sake of his mortal children.

'These are the lesser mysteries of love, into which even you, Socrates, may enter. As for the greater and more hidden ones, which are the crown of these and to which these will lead if pursued in the right spirit, I do not know whether you will be able to attain them. But I will do my utmost to teach you, and you must follow if you can. Whoever wants to go about this matter rightly should begin in youth by visiting beautiful forms. First, if his guide leads him rightly, he should love one such form only, and out of that love create beautiful thoughts. Soon he will see for himself that the beauty of one form is closely related to the beauty of another. Then, if beauty of form in general is what he pursues, how foolish he would be not to recognize that the beauty in every form is one and the same! When he sees this, he will relax his violent love for the one, which he will despise and think a small thing, and he will become a lover of all beautiful forms. In the next stage he will consider the beauty of the mind more honorable than the beauty of the outward form.

So if someone with a virtuous soul has only a little charm, he will be content to love and care for him. He will seek out and bring to birth thoughts that may improve the young, until he is compelled to contemplate the beauty of institutions and laws. He will see that the beauty of them all is of one family, and that personal beauty is a trifle. After laws and institutions he will go on to the sciences, so that he may see their beauty. He will no longer be like a servant in love with the beauty of one youth or man or institution, himself a slave, mean and narrow-minded. Instead he will be drawing toward and contemplating the vast sea of beauty, and in boundless love of wisdom he will create many beautiful and noble thoughts and ideas. There on that shore he grows and gains strength, until at last the vision is revealed to him of a single science, the science of beauty everywhere. I will go on to this now, so please give me your very best attention:

'Whoever has been taught this far in the things of love, and has learned to see the beautiful in due order and succession, will suddenly, as he comes toward the end, perceive a nature of wondrous beauty (and this, Socrates, is the final cause of all our earlier toils). First, this nature is everlasting: it does not grow or decay, or wax or wane. Second, it is not beautiful in one respect and ugly in another, or beautiful at one time or in one relation or in one place, and ugly at another time or in another relation or in another place, as if beautiful to some and ugly to others. Nor will it appear to him in the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the body, or in any form of speech or knowledge, or as existing in any other being, such as an animal, or in heaven, or in earth, or in any other place. It is beauty absolute, separate, simple and everlasting, which is shared by the ever-growing and perishing beauties of all other things without itself diminishing or increasing or changing at all. Whoever has climbed up from these things under the influence of true love, and begins to perceive that beauty, is not far from the end.

'And the true order of going, or of being led by another, to the things of love is this: to begin from the beauties of earth and mount upward for the sake of that other beauty, using these as steps only. He goes from one to two, and from two to all beautiful forms, and from beautiful forms to beautiful practices, and from beautiful practices to beautiful ideas, until from beautiful ideas he arrives at the idea of absolute beauty, and at last knows what the essence of beauty is. This, my dear Socrates,' said the stranger from Mantineia, 'is the life above all others that a man should live, in the contemplation of absolute beauty. If you once saw it, you would find that it cannot be measured by gold or garments or beautiful boys and youths, whose presence now entrances you. You and many others would be content to live seeing them only and talking with them, without food or drink, if that were possible. You only want to look at them and be with them. But what if a man had eyes to see the true beauty, the divine beauty, I mean, pure and clear and unmixed, not clogged with the pollutions of mortality and all the colors and vanities of human life? What if he looked at that, and held converse with the true beauty, simple and divine?

Remember that only in that communion, beholding beauty with the eye of the mind, will he be able to bring forth not images of beauty but realities (for he is holding not an image but a reality). By bringing forth and nourishing true virtue he will become the friend of God and be immortal, if any mortal can. Would that be an ignoble life?'

Such, Phaedrus, were the words of Diotima, and I speak not only to you but to all of you. I am convinced they are true. And being convinced, I try to convince others that, in reaching this end, human nature will not easily find a better helper than love. Therefore I also say that every man ought to honor him as I honor him myself, and follow his ways, and urge others to do the same, and praise the power and spirit of love as well as I am able, now and always.
You may call the words I have spoken, Phaedrus, an encomium of love, or anything else you please.

chapters.title: Alcibiades
paragraphs: Socrates finished speaking, and the company applauded. Aristophanes was about to answer the allusion Socrates had made to his own speech, when suddenly there was a loud knocking at the front door, like a band of revelers, and they heard the sound of a flute-girl. Agathon told the attendants to go and see who the intruders were. 'If they are friends of ours,' he said, 'invite them in. If not, say that the drinking is over.' A little while later they heard the voice of Alcibiades booming in the courtyard. He was very drunk, and he kept roaring and shouting, 'Where is Agathon? Take me to Agathon!' At last, held up by the flute-girl and some of his attendants, he made his way to them. 'Greetings, friends,' he said, standing in the doorway with a thick garland of ivy and violets on his head and ribbons streaming down from it. 'Will you take a very drunken man as a companion in your drinking? Or shall I crown Agathon, which is why I came, and go away? I could not come yesterday, so I am here today, with these ribbons on my head. I want to take them from my own head and crown the head of this most beautiful and most wise of men, if I may call him that. Will you laugh at me because I am drunk? Yet I know very well that I am speaking the truth, even if you laugh. But first tell me: if I come in, will we have the understanding I spoke of (supra Will you have a very drunken man? etc.)?
Will you drink with me or not?'

The company loudly begged him to come in and take a place among them, and Agathon in particular invited him. So the people with him led him in. As he was being led, meaning to crown Agathon, he took the ribbons from his own head and held them in front of his eyes. This kept him from seeing Socrates, who made room for him. Alcibiades took the empty place between Agathon and Socrates, and as he sat down he embraced Agathon and crowned him. Take off his sandals, said Agathon, and let him make a third on the same couch.

By all means; but who is our third partner in the drinking? said Alcibiades, turning around and starting up as he caught sight of Socrates. By Heracles, he said, what is this? Here is Socrates, always lying in wait for me, and always, as is his way, popping up in the most unexpected places! Now, what have you to say for yourself? And why are you lying here, where I see you have managed to find a place, not next to a joker or a lover of jokes, like Aristophanes, but next to the most beautiful man in the company?

Socrates turned to Agathon and said: I must ask you to protect me, Agathon, because this man's passion has become a serious problem for me. Ever since I became his admirer, I have not been allowed to speak to any other beautiful person, or even to look at one. If I do, he goes wild with envy and jealousy, and not only abuses me but can hardly keep his hands off me, and right now he may do me some harm. Please see to this, and either reconcile me with him or, if he turns violent, protect me, since I am in physical fear of his mad and passionate attacks.

There can never be a reconciliation between you and me, said Alcibiades; but for now I will put off your punishment. And I must ask you, Agathon, to give me back some of the ribbons, so that I may crown the marvelous head of this universal despot. I would not want him to complain that I crowned you and neglected him, who in conversation defeats all mankind, and not just once, as you did the day before yesterday, but always. With that, he took some of the ribbons, crowned Socrates, and lay back again.

Then he said: You seem to be sober, my friends, and that cannot be endured. You must drink, since that was the agreement under which I was let in, and I appoint myself master of the feast until you are well drunk. Let us have a large goblet, Agathon, or rather, he said, turning to the attendant, bring me that wine-cooler. The wine-cooler that had caught his eye was a vessel holding more than two quarts. He filled it and emptied it, and told the attendant to fill it again for Socrates. Notice, my friends, said Alcibiades, that this clever trick of mine will have no effect on Socrates, for he can drink any amount of wine and be no closer to drunk. Socrates drank the cup the attendant filled for him.
Eryximachus said: What is this, Alcibiades? Are we to have neither conversation nor singing over our cups, but simply drink as if we were thirsty?
Alcibiades replied: Greetings, worthy son of a most wise and worthy father!
The same to you, said Eryximachus; but what shall we do?
I leave that to you, said Alcibiades.
'The wise physician skilled our wounds to heal (from Pope's Homer, Il.)'
will prescribe, and we will obey. What do you want?

Well, said Eryximachus, before you arrived we had agreed that each of us in turn should make a speech in praise of love, as good a one as he could. The turn went around from left to right. All of us have spoken, and you have not spoken but have drunk well, so you ought to speak. Then you may set Socrates any task you please, and he may do the same to the man on his right, and so on.

That is good, Eryximachus, said Alcibiades; and yet it is hardly fair to compare a drunken man's speech with those of sober men. And I should like to know, my dear friend, whether you really believe what Socrates was just saying. I can assure you that the very opposite is true, and that if I praise anyone but him in his presence, whether God or man, he will hardly keep his hands off me.
Shame on you, said Socrates.
Be quiet, said Alcibiades, for by Poseidon, there is no one else I will praise while you are in the company.
Well then, said Eryximachus, if you like, praise Socrates.
What do you think, Eryximachus? said Alcibiades. Shall I attack him and punish him in front of you all?
What are you up to? said Socrates. Are you going to get a laugh at my expense? Is that what your praise means?
I am going to speak the truth, if you will allow me.
I not only allow it, I urge you to speak the truth.

Then I will begin at once, said Alcibiades. And if I say anything untrue, you may interrupt me, if you like, and say 'that is a lie,' though my intention is to speak the truth. But you must not be surprised if I speak in no particular order, as things come into my mind. A fluent and orderly list of all your oddities is not an easy task for a man in my condition.

And now, my boys, I shall praise Socrates in a comparison that will seem to him a caricature, and yet I speak not to make fun of him but only for the sake of the truth. I say that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus that stand in the sculptors' shops, holding pipes and flutes in their mouths. They are made to open down the middle, and they have images of gods inside them. I say also that he is like Marsyas the satyr. You yourself will not deny, Socrates, that your face is like a satyr's. Yes, and the resemblance goes further. For example, you are a bully, as I can prove by witnesses if you will not confess it. And are you not a flute-player? You are, and a far more wonderful performer than Marsyas. He used instruments to charm the souls of men by the power of his breath, and those who play his music still do so. For the melodies of Olympus (compare Arist. Pol.) come from Marsyas, who taught them, and whether a great master plays them or a miserable flute-girl, they have a power that no other music has. They alone take possession of the soul and reveal the needs of those who want gods and mysteries, because they are divine. But you produce the same effect with your words alone, and do not need the flute. That is the difference between you and him.

When we hear any other speaker, even a very good one, he has no effect on us at all, or not much. But the mere fragments of you and your words, even at second hand and however badly repeated, amaze and possess the souls of every man, woman, and child who comes within hearing of them. And if I were not afraid that you would think me hopelessly drunk, I would swear an oath as well as speak, to tell you the influence they have always had on me and still have. For my heart leaps more than that of any Corybantian reveler, and my eyes pour out tears when I hear them. And I see that many others are affected in the same way. I have heard Pericles and other great orators, and I thought they spoke well, but I never had any feeling like this. My soul was not stirred by them, and I was not angry at the thought of my own slavish condition. But this Marsyas has often brought me to the point where I felt I could hardly endure the life I am leading (you will admit this, Socrates). And I know that if I did not shut my ears against him and flee, as from the voice of the siren, my fate would be the same as that of others: he would pin me down, and I would grow old sitting at his feet. For he makes me admit that I ought not to live as I do, neglecting the needs of my own soul and busying myself with the affairs of the Athenians. So I hold my ears and tear myself away from him.

And he is the only person who ever made me ashamed, which you might think is not in my nature, and no one else does the same. For I know that I cannot answer him or say that I ought not to do as he tells me. But when I leave his presence, the love of popularity gets the better of me. So I run away from him, and when I see him again I am ashamed of what I admitted to him. Many a time I have wished him dead, and yet I know that I would be much more sorry than glad if he were to die. So I am at my wit's end.

This is what I and many others have suffered from the flute-playing of this satyr. Yet hear me once more, while I show you how exact the comparison is and how marvelous his power. For let me tell you, none of you know him; but I will reveal him to you, since I have begun and must go on. Do you see how fond he is of beautiful people? He is always with them and is always being struck by them, and yet he knows nothing and is ignorant of everything. That is the appearance he puts on. Is he not like a Silenus in this? He certainly is. His outer mask is the carved head of the Silenus; but, my fellow drinkers, when he is opened, what self-control lives inside! Know that beauty and wealth and honor, which the many admire, are of no account to him and are utterly despised by him. He pays no attention at all to the people who have them. Mankind is nothing to him, and he spends his whole life mocking and scorning them. But when I opened him and looked inside at his serious purpose, I saw in him divine and golden images of such fascinating beauty that I was ready to do at once whatever Socrates commanded. Others may have missed them, but I saw them. Now I imagined that he was seriously in love with my beauty, and I thought that this would give me a grand opportunity to hear him tell what he knew, for I had a wonderful opinion of the attractions of my youth.

To carry out this plan, the next time I went to him I sent away the attendant who usually accompanied me (I will confess the whole truth, and I ask you to listen; and if I speak falsely, Socrates, expose the falsehood). So he and I were alone together, and I thought that with nobody else there I would hear him speak the language lovers use to their beloveds when they are alone, and I was delighted. Nothing of the sort happened. He talked as usual, spent the day with me, and then went away. Afterward I challenged him to the palaestra, and he wrestled and grappled with me several times with no one else present. I thought I might succeed that way. Not a bit of it; I got nowhere with him. Finally, since I had failed so far, I decided I must take stronger measures and attack him boldly. Having begun, I would not give him up, but find out how matters stood between him and me. So I invited him to dinner, just as if he were a beautiful youth and I a scheming lover. He was not easily persuaded to come. After a while, however, he accepted the invitation, and the first time he came he wanted to leave right after dinner, and I did not have the nerve to keep him. The second time, still following my plan, after we had eaten I kept conversing far into the night, and when he wanted to go, I pretended that the hour was late and that he had much better stay.

So he lay down on the couch next to me, the same one on which he had eaten, and no one but the two of us was sleeping in the room. All this can be told without shame to anyone. But what follows I could hardly tell you if I were sober. Yet as the proverb says, 'In vino veritas,' whether with boys or without them (In allusion to two proverbs.); and so I must speak. Nor would I be justified in hiding the lofty actions of Socrates when I come to praise him. Besides, I have felt the serpent's sting; and he who has suffered, as they say, is willing to tell his fellow sufferers only, since they alone are likely to understand him, and will not judge harshly the words or deeds that his agony has wrung from him. For I have been bitten by something worse than a viper's tooth. I have known in my soul, or in my heart, or in some other part, the worst of pangs, more violent in a generous youth than any serpent's tooth: the pang of philosophy, which will make a man say or do anything. And you whom I see around me, Phaedrus and Agathon and Eryximachus and Pausanias and Aristodemus and Aristophanes, all of you, and I need not mention Socrates himself, have experienced the same madness and passion in your longing for wisdom. So listen, and forgive what I did then and what I say now. But let the attendants and any other uninitiated and ill-mannered persons close the doors of their ears.

When the lamp was put out and the servants had gone away, I thought I must be plain with him and have no more ambiguity. So I gave him a shake and said: 'Socrates, are you asleep?' 'No,' he said. 'Do you know what I am thinking about?' 'What are you thinking about?' he said. 'I think,' I replied, 'that of all the lovers I have ever had, you are the only one worthy of me, and you seem to be too modest to speak. Now I feel that I would be a fool to refuse you this or any other favor, and so I come to lay at your feet all that I have and all that my friends have, in the hope that you will help me toward virtue, which I desire above all things, and in which I believe you can help me better than anyone else. And I would certainly have more reason to be ashamed of what wise men would say if I refused a favor to someone like you, than of what the world, which is mostly fools, would say of me if I granted it.' To these words he replied in the ironical manner so characteristic of him: 'Alcibiades, my friend, you certainly have a lofty aim, if what you say is true, and if there really is some power in me by which you could become better. You must see in me some rare beauty, of a kind infinitely higher than any I see in you. And so, if you mean to share with me and to exchange beauty for beauty, you will have the great advantage of me. You will gain true beauty in return for appearance, like Diomede, gold in exchange for brass.

But look again, my dear friend, and see whether you are not deceived in me. The mind begins to see clearly when the bodily eye grows dim, and it will be a long time before you get old.' Hearing this, I said: 'I have told you my purpose, which is quite serious, so consider what you think best for you and me.' 'That is good,' he said; 'at some other time, then, we will consider and act as seems best about this and about other matters.' At that, I thought he was struck, and that the words I had let fly like arrows had wounded him. So without waiting to hear more, I got up, threw my coat over him, and crept under his threadbare cloak, since it was winter, and there I lay the whole night with this wonderful monster in my arms. This again, Socrates, you will not deny. And yet, in spite of everything, he was so far above my advances, so contemptuous and mocking and disdainful of my beauty, which I really thought had some attractions. Hear this, O judges, for you shall be judges of the haughty virtue of Socrates. Nothing more happened, but in the morning when I woke (let all the gods and goddesses be my witnesses) I got up as if from the bed of a father or an elder brother.

What do you suppose my feelings were, after this rejection, at the thought of my own dishonor? And yet I could not help marveling at his natural self-control and self-restraint and manliness. I never imagined I could meet a man like him in wisdom and endurance. So I could not be angry with him or give up his company, any more than I could hope to win him. For I knew well that if Ajax could not be wounded by steel, much less could he be moved by money, and my one chance of captivating him by my looks had failed. So I was at my wit's end; no one was ever more hopelessly enslaved by another. All this happened before he and I went on the expedition to Potidaea. There we shared a mess, and I had the chance to observe his extraordinary power of enduring hardship. His endurance was simply marvelous when we were cut off from our supplies and had to go without food. On such occasions, which often happen in war, he was superior not only to me but to everybody; no one could be compared to him. Yet at a festival he was the only person who really knew how to enjoy himself. Though he was unwilling to drink, he could, if compelled, beat us all at that, and, wonderful to relate, no human being had ever seen Socrates drunk. His powers, if I am not mistaken, will be tested before long. His fortitude in enduring cold was also surprising.

There was a severe frost, for the winter in that region is truly terrible. Everybody else either stayed indoors or, if they went out, wore an amazing amount of clothing, with good shoes and their feet wrapped in felt and fleeces. In the midst of this, Socrates, with bare feet on the ice and in his ordinary clothes, marched better than the soldiers who had shoes, and they looked daggers at him because he seemed to despise them.
I have told you one tale, and now I must tell you another, which is worth hearing,
'Of the doings and sufferings of the enduring man'

while he was on the expedition. One morning he was thinking about something he could not resolve. He would not give it up but kept thinking from early dawn until noon. There he stood, fixed in thought, and at noon people noticed him, and the rumor ran through the astonished crowd that Socrates had been standing and thinking about something ever since daybreak. At last, in the evening after supper, some Ionians out of curiosity (I should explain that this was not in winter but in summer) brought out their mats and slept in the open air so that they could watch him and see whether he would stand all night. He stood there until the next morning, and when the light returned he offered a prayer to the sun and went on his way (compare supra). I will also tell, if you please, and indeed I am bound to tell, of his courage in battle. For who but he saved my life? This was the engagement in which I received the prize for valor. I was wounded and he would not leave me, but rescued me and my arms. He ought to have received the prize for valor which the generals wanted to give me, partly because of my rank, and I told them so (this, again, Socrates will not challenge or deny); but he was more eager than the generals that I, and not he, should have the prize.

There was another occasion on which his behavior was very remarkable: in the flight of the army after the battle of Delium, where he served among the heavy-armed. I had a better chance to watch him than at Potidaea, for I was on horseback and so comparatively out of danger. He and Laches were retreating, for the troops were in flight, and I met them and told them not to lose heart, and promised to stay with them. There you could see him, Aristophanes, just as you describe him (Aristoph. Clouds), exactly as he is in the streets of Athens, stalking like a pelican and rolling his eyes, calmly eyeing enemies and friends alike, and making it very clear to anybody, even from a distance, that whoever attacked him would meet with stout resistance. In this way he and his companion escaped, for this is the sort of man who is never touched in war; those who are pursued are only the ones running away headlong. I particularly noticed how far he surpassed Laches in presence of mind. There are many marvels I could tell in praise of Socrates. Most of his ways might perhaps be matched in another man, but his complete unlikeness to any human being who is or ever has been is truly astonishing.

You may imagine Brasidas and others to have been like Achilles, or you may imagine Nestor and Antenor to have been like Pericles, and the same may be said of other famous men. But of this strange being you will never be able to find any likeness, however remote, either among men now living or among those of the past, except the one I have already suggested, of Silenus and the satyrs; and they represent in a figure not only the man himself but his words. For although I forgot to mention it before, his words are like the images of Silenus that open. They are ridiculous when you first hear them. He dresses himself in language like the skin of the wanton satyr, for his talk is of pack-asses and smiths and cobblers and tanners, and he is always repeating the same things in the same words (compare Gorg.), so that any ignorant or inexperienced person might be inclined to laugh at him. But anyone who opens the bust and sees what is inside will find that his are the only words with any meaning in them, and also the most divine, full of beautiful images of virtue, and of the widest reach, or rather extending to the whole duty of a good and honorable man.

This, friends, is my praise of Socrates. I have added my blame of him for his ill-treatment of me. And he has ill-treated not only me but Charmides the son of Glaucon, and Euthydemus the son of Diocles, and many others in the same way. He begins as their lover and ends by making them pay court to him. So I say to you, Agathon, 'Do not be deceived by him; learn from me and take warning, and do not be a fool and learn by experience, as the proverb says.'

When Alcibiades had finished, there was a laugh at his frankness, for he seemed to be still in love with Socrates. You are sober, Alcibiades, said Socrates, or you would never have gone such a roundabout way to hide the purpose of your satyr's praises. All this long story is only a clever circumlocution, and the point comes in by the way at the end. You want to start a quarrel between me and Agathon, and your idea is that I ought to love you and nobody else, and that you and you alone ought to love Agathon. But the plot of this Satyric or Silenic drama has been detected, and you must not let him, Agathon, set us at odds.

I believe you are right, said Agathon, and I am inclined to think that his intention in placing himself between you and me was only to divide us. But he shall gain nothing by that move, for I will go and lie on the couch next to you.
Yes, yes, replied Socrates, by all means come here and lie on the couch below me.
Alas, said Alcibiades, how this man fools me! He is determined to get the better of me at every turn. I beg you, let Agathon lie between us.

Certainly not, said Socrates. You have praised me, and I in turn ought to praise my neighbor on the right. He would be out of order in praising me again when he ought rather to be praised by me. I must ask you to agree to this, and not be jealous, for I have a great desire to praise the youth.
Hurrah! cried Agathon, I will get up at once, so that Socrates may praise me.
The usual way, said Alcibiades; where Socrates is, no one else has any chance with the beautiful. And see how readily he has found a plausible reason to draw Agathon to himself.

Agathon got up to take his place on the couch beside Socrates, when suddenly a band of revelers entered and ruined the order of the banquet. Someone who was going out had left the door open, and they had found their way in and made themselves at home. Great confusion followed, and everyone was forced to drink large quantities of wine. Aristodemus said that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and others went away, while he himself fell asleep and, since the nights were long, slept well. Toward daybreak he was woken by the crowing of cocks. When he woke, the others were either asleep or had gone away. Only Socrates, Aristophanes, and Agathon remained, drinking from a large goblet which they passed around, and Socrates was talking with them. Aristodemus was only half awake and did not hear the beginning of the talk. The main thing he remembered was Socrates forcing the other two to admit that the genius of comedy was the same as that of tragedy, and that the true artist in tragedy was an artist in comedy also. They were drowsy and did not quite follow the argument, and so they were compelled to agree. First Aristophanes dropped off, and then, when day was already dawning, Agathon. Socrates, having put them to sleep, got up to leave, and Aristodemus, as was his habit, followed him. At the Lyceum he took a bath and spent the day as usual. In the evening he went home and went to rest.
